# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I focus on the north region subsample, where the data are most comparable, control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 0.218 (SE 0.408, p = 0.5934, N = 684).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
pre='log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(sector)+listed+C(region)'
for name,f,df in [('raw','productivity_2023~training_hours',d),('basic','productivity_2023~training_hours+log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020',d),('full','productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre,d)]+[('reg_'+r,'productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre.replace('+C(region)',''),d[d.region==r]) for r in ['north','central','south']]:
    m=smf.ols(f,df).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(name,len(df),m.params['training_hours'],m.bse['training_hours'],m.pvalues['training_hours'])
print(d.isna().sum().sum())

content.text:
I rejected the report. Its "no effect" conclusion comes from restricting the sample to the north region, which the report doesn't justify, and the full data show a clear positive effect.

I re-ran the regressions on `data.csv` with the same robust (HC1) standard errors. The coefficients below are the effect of `training_hours` on `productivity_2023`:

| Sample | N | Coefficient | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| North only (the report's sample), 2020 productivity and firm size and age as controls, outcome trimmed | 684 | 0.218 | 0.59 |
| All regions, no controls | 2000 | 2.37 | <0.001 |
| All regions, same controls as the report | 2000 | 0.80 | <0.001 |
| All regions, all 2020 firm characteristics as controls | 2000 | 0.84 | <0.001 |
| North only, all 2020 firm characteristics as controls | 698 | 0.34 | 0.43 |
| Central only, same full controls | 617 | 0.46 | 0.28 |
| South only, same full controls | 685 | 1.86 | <0.001 |

The effect is strongest in the south, so the north-only null reflects the subgroup chosen, not the whole data. The report also says it estimated one specification, without mentioning that the other regions give different results.

I wrote the verdict to `verdict.json`.
